steps.text: In the lesson “Polynomial Interpolation” you saw: a high-degree polynomial through many equally spaced points oscillates wildly at the edges (Runge's phenomenon). What do you do with 50 or 1000 data points?
steps.explanation:
The idea: instead of a single high-degree polynomial, use many low-degree polynomials – one for each subinterval between two neighbouring points.

Such a function assembled piecewise from polynomials is called a spline.

Each piece only “sees” its neighbourhood. An outlier at one point therefore hardly affects distant points – quite unlike a global polynomial.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Piecewise instead of in one piece
steps.insight: Spline: piecewise low-degree polynomials instead of one high-degree polynomial.

steps.text: The name comes from shipbuilding. To draw smooth curves for ship hulls, designers used a flexible strip of wood called a “spline”.
steps.explanation:
The strip was held in place at some points by weights and bent in between into the most “relaxed” shape by itself – with as little bending energy as possible.

Remarkably, the mathematical cubic splines of this lesson describe exactly this shape. Today splines are in every drawing program, in fonts, in CAD systems and in computer graphics.

Our roadmap:
1. Linear splines: simple, but with kinks
2. Cubic splines: which conditions are needed?
3. The moment method: a linear system for the curvatures
4. Examples by hand
5. Solving efficiently: the tridiagonal system
6. Why splines are so good: minimal property and error
steps.section: Chapter 1 · Piecewise instead of in one piece
steps.insight: Cubic splines are the mathematical version of a flexible drawing strip.

steps.text: The simplest spline: connect neighbouring points by straight lines. This is the linear spline or polygonal line.
steps.formula: s(x) = y_i + \frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{x_{i+1} - x_i}\,(x - x_i) \qquad \text{for } x \in [x_i, x_{i+1}]
steps.explanation:
On each subinterval this is linear interpolation between two points.

Example: points \((0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0)\). At \(x = 0.5\) we are in the first piece: \(s(0.5) = 0 + 1 \cdot 0.5 = 0.5\). At \(x = 1.5\) in the second: \(s(1.5) = 1 - 1 \cdot 0.5 = 0.5\).

You know this from every line chart in a spreadsheet.
steps.insight: Linear spline: connect the points by straight lines.

steps.text: How accurate is the linear spline? On each subinterval it is an interpolating polynomial of degree 1. With the error formula from the last lesson:
steps.explanation:
The factor \(\frac{h^2}{8}\) comes from \(\frac{1}{2!} \cdot \max |(x - x_i)(x - x_{i+1})| = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{h^2}{4}\).

Example: \(\sin x\) on \([0, \pi]\) with 4 subintervals (\(h = \frac{\pi}{4}\)):
• Bound: \(\frac{(\pi/4)^2}{8} \cdot 1 \approx 0.077\)
• Actual: \(0.070\)

With 8 subintervals: \(0.019\), with 16: \(0.0048\). Half the step size – a quarter of the error. We say the error is of order \(O(h^2)\).
steps.insight: Linear spline: error \(\le \frac{h^2}{8}\max|f''|\). Halving the step size quarters the error.

steps.text: The linear spline has a flaw: it has kinks at the nodes.
steps.explanation:
In the example \((0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0)\) the slope to the left of \(x = 1\) is \(+1\), to the right \(-1\). The derivative jumps.

For many applications this is unacceptable:
• A roller coaster with kinks would shake its passengers.
• A robot arm whose velocity jumps gets infinitely large accelerations.
• A car body with kinks does not look good – and reflects light badly.

So one wants a curve that is not only continuous but also has smooth transitions in slope and curvature.
steps.insight: Linear splines have kinks. Smooth curves need higher-degree polynomials on the pieces.

steps.text: Quick check: a linear spline is to approximate \(e^{x}\) on \([0, 1]\) with error at most \(10^{-4}\). How many subintervals are needed?
steps.explanation:
\(\max |f''| = e \approx 2.72\). We need \(\frac{h^2}{8} \cdot 2.72 \le 10^{-4}\).

\(h^2 \le \frac{8 \cdot 10^{-4}}{2.72} \approx 2.94 \cdot 10^{-4}\), so \(h \le 0.0171\).

That is \(\frac{1}{0.0171} \approx 58.3\), so at least 59 subintervals.

A lot – cubic splines need considerably fewer for the same accuracy, as we will see.
steps.insight: For high accuracy the linear spline needs very many nodes.

steps.text: A cubic spline through the points \((x_0, y_0), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\) is a function \(s\) with:
steps.explanation:
Condition (3) means: at each interior node the value, slope and curvature of the left and right pieces agree. The curve has no kinks and no jumps in curvature – the seams cannot be seen with the naked eye.

Why degree 3? With degree 2 there is too little freedom to match slope and curvature. Degree 3 is the smallest degree that satisfies everything – and it describes exactly the bent wooden strip.
steps.insight: Cubic spline: piecewise cubic, interpolates the points, \(s\), \(s'\), \(s''\) continuous.

steps.text: Are these conditions enough to determine the spline uniquely? Let's count for \(n\) subintervals:
steps.formula:
\begin{array}{l|c}
\text{unknowns: } n \text{ pieces} \times 4 \text{ coefficients} & 4n \\ \hline
\text{interpolation: each piece at both ends} & 2n \\
s' \text{ continuous at the } n - 1 \text{ interior nodes} & n - 1 \\
s'' \text{ continuous at the } n - 1 \text{ interior nodes} & n - 1 \\ \hline
\text{total conditions} & 4n - 2
\end{array}
steps.explanation:
Exactly 2 conditions are missing. That is not a mistake but a freedom: you may prescribe something at the two ends.

With the wooden strip: you can leave the ends free or clamp them in a particular direction. Both give a sensible curve, but different ones.
steps.insight: Cubic splines have \(4n\) unknowns and \(4n - 2\) conditions. The two missing ones are boundary conditions.

steps.text: The most common boundary conditions:
steps.explanation:
• Natural spline: \(s''(x_0) = 0\) and \(s''(x_n) = 0\). The curve is not curved at the ends – like a wooden strip with free ends. The standard case when nothing else is known.

• Clamped (complete) spline: \(s'(x_0)\) and \(s'(x_n)\) are prescribed, for example as known derivatives of \(f\). More accurate if the derivatives are known.

• Periodic spline: \(s'\) and \(s''\) agree at the start and end. For periodic data, for example a daily cycle or a closed curve.

• Not-a-knot: the first and second pieces are the same polynomial (likewise at the end). The default in MATLAB if nothing is specified.

In this lesson we compute with the natural spline.
steps.insight: Boundary conditions: natural (\(s'' = 0\) at the ends), clamped (\(s'\) given), periodic, not-a-knot.

steps.text: Quick check: a cubic spline is to pass through 4 points. How many unknowns does it have, and how many conditions of each kind are there?
steps.explanation:
4 points ⇒ \(n = 3\) subintervals ⇒ \(4 \cdot 3 = 12\) unknowns.

Conditions:
• Interpolation: \(2 \cdot 3 = 6\)
• \(s'\) continuous at 2 interior nodes: \(2\)
• \(s''\) continuous at 2 interior nodes: \(2\)
• Boundary conditions: \(2\)

Together \(6 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12\) ✓ – exactly as many as unknowns.

Solving a linear system with 12 unknowns by hand would be tedious. The moment method in the next chapter reduces it to 2 unknowns.
steps.insight: As many conditions as unknowns – but organised cleverly, the system becomes much smaller.

steps.text: The trick of the moment method: compute not with the coefficients but with the curvatures at the nodes, the so-called moments:
steps.explanation:
Why is that clever? On each subinterval \(s\) is cubic, so \(s''\) is linear. A linear function is determined by its values at the two ends: \(M_i\) and \(M_{i+1}\).

Once all moments are known, each piece can be written down directly (by integrating twice; the integration constants follow from \(s(x_i) = y_i\) and \(s(x_{i+1}) = y_{i+1}\)).

The name “moment” comes from mechanics: in a bent beam the curvature is proportional to the bending moment.

For the natural spline simply \(M_0 = 0\) and \(M_n = 0\).
steps.insight: Moments \(M_i = s''(x_i)\): whoever knows the curvatures at the nodes knows the whole spline.

steps.text: For equally spaced nodes (spacing \(h\)) the piece on \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\) with \(t = x - x_i\) reads:
steps.explanation:
Let's check that the piece satisfies the conditions:
• At \(t = 0\): \(s_i = y_i\) ✓
• \(s_i'' = M_i + \frac{M_{i+1} - M_i}{h}\,t\). At \(t = 0\): \(M_i\) ✓, at \(t = h\): \(M_{i+1}\) ✓
• At \(t = h\): \(y_i + b_i h + \frac{M_i}{2}h^2 + \frac{M_{i+1} - M_i}{6}h^2\). Plugging in \(b_i\) gives exactly \(y_{i+1}\) ✓

Interpolation and continuous curvature are thus satisfied automatically. Only the continuous slope at the interior nodes is still missing.
steps.insight: With this formula the pieces automatically satisfy interpolation and continuity of \(s''\).

steps.text: The last condition: the slope of the left piece at node \(x_i\) must equal the slope of the right piece. Worked out, this gives for each interior node:
steps.explanation:
These are the moment equations: \(n - 1\) linear equations for the \(n - 1\) unknown moments \(M_1, \ldots, M_{n-1}\) (for the natural spline \(M_0 = M_n = 0\)).

The right-hand side has a vivid meaning: \(\frac{y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1}}{h^2}\) is an approximation of the second derivative (the central second-order difference quotient). So the equation roughly says: the weighted curvature of the spline matches the “curvature of the data”.

From 12 unknowns (with 4 points) only 2 remain.
steps.insight: Moment equations: \(M_{i-1} + 4M_i + M_{i+1} = \frac{6}{h^2}(y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1})\).

steps.text: The recipe for a natural cubic spline with equally spaced nodes:
steps.explanation:
1. Set \(M_0 = 0\) and \(M_n = 0\).
2. For each interior node compute the right-hand side \(\frac{6}{h^2}(y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1})\).
3. Solve the linear system for \(M_1, \ldots, M_{n-1}\).
4. For each piece compute \(b_i = \frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h} - \frac{h}{6}(2M_i + M_{i+1})\).
5. Write down the pieces \(s_i(x) = y_i + b_i t + \frac{M_i}{2}t^2 + \frac{M_{i+1} - M_i}{6h}t^3\) with \(t = x - x_i\).

For unequally spaced nodes there are similar formulas with the individual spacings \(h_i\).
steps.insight: Spline recipe: moments from the linear system, then the pieces with the standard formula.

steps.text: First example: the natural spline through \((0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0)\). Here \(h = 1\), and there is only one interior node.
steps.explanation:
With \(M_0 = M_2 = 0\) a single equation remains.

The negative moment fits: in the middle the curve is curved downwards (like a hill).

Now the pieces:
• \(b_0 = \frac{1 - 0}{1} - \frac{1}{6}(0 - 3) = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5\)
• \(s_0(x) = 0 + 1.5x + 0 + \frac{-3 - 0}{6}x^3 = 1.5x - 0.5x^3\) on \([0, 1]\)

By symmetry \(s_1(x) = s_0(2 - x)\) on \([1, 2]\).
steps.insight: One interior node = one moment equation.

steps.text: Let's check the conditions for \(s_0(x) = 1.5x - 0.5x^3\):
steps.explanation:
The slope at the middle node is \(0\) – by symmetry the same holds for the right piece. So the slope is continuous ✓

Comparison at \(x = 0.5\):
• Spline: \(s_0(0.5) = 0.75 - 0.0625 = 0.6875\)
• Linear spline: \(0.5\)
• Parabola through the three points (\(p(x) = 2x - x^2\)): \(0.75\)

The spline lies between the polygonal line and the parabola – a gentle curve without a kink.
steps.insight: Always check: values at the nodes, equal slopes, zero curvature at the ends.

steps.text: Second example with two interior nodes: points \((0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0), (3, 1)\), \(h = 1\).
steps.explanation:
A \(2 \times 2\) system. From the first equation: \(M_2 = -12 - 4M_1\). Substituting into the second:
\(M_1 + 4(-12 - 4M_1) = 12 \Rightarrow -15M_1 = 60 \Rightarrow M_1 = -4\)

Then \(M_2 = -12 + 16 = 4\).

Moments: \(M = (0, -4, 4, 0)\). At \(x = 1\) (hill) curved downwards, at \(x = 2\) (valley) upwards – matching the shape of the data.
steps.insight: The sign of the moments shows whether the curve bends up or down at a node.

steps.text: The three pieces of this spline:
steps.explanation:
Computation for \(s_0\): \(b_0 = 1 - \frac{1}{6}(0 - 4) = \frac{5}{3}\), cubic coefficient \(\frac{-4 - 0}{6} = -\frac{2}{3}\).

Computation for \(s_2\): \(b_2 = (1 - 0) - \frac{1}{6}(2 \cdot 4 + 0) = -\frac{1}{3}\), quadratic coefficient \(\frac{4}{2} = 2\), cubic \(\frac{0 - 4}{6} = -\frac{2}{3}\).

Evaluation at \(x = 2.5\) (i.e. \(t = 0.5\) in \(s_2\)): \(-\frac{1}{6} + 0.5 - \frac{1}{12} = 0.25\).

The animation shows the three pieces in different colours. No transition can be seen at the seams.
steps.insight: Each piece is its own cubic polynomial – together they form a smooth curve.

steps.text: Comparison with the degree-3 interpolating polynomial through the same four points:
steps.explanation:
The polynomial through \((0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0), (3, 1)\) is \(p(x) = \frac{2}{3}x^3 - 3x^2 + \frac{10}{3}x\).

At \(x = 0.5\):
• Polynomial: \(p(0.5) = \frac{1}{12} - \frac{3}{4} + \frac{5}{3} = 1.0\)
• Spline: \(s(0.5) = \frac{5}{6} - \frac{1}{12} = 0.75\)

Between the first two points the polynomial shoots up to \(1.0\) – beyond the highest data value. The spline stays more restrained. In the last picture of the animation you see the polynomial dashed for comparison.

With four points the difference is still small. With 20 points the polynomial would be useless, the spline would not.
steps.insight: The spline oscillates less than the interpolating polynomial through the same points.

steps.text: Quick check: determine the moment \(M_1\) of the natural spline through \((0, 1), (2, 3), (4, 1)\). Careful: here \(h = 2\).
steps.explanation:
One interior node, \(M_0 = M_2 = 0\):
\(4M_1 = \frac{6}{h^2}(y_0 - 2y_1 + y_2) = \frac{6}{4}(1 - 6 + 1) = \frac{6}{4} \cdot (-4) = -6\)

So \(M_1 = -1.5\).

Typical mistake: forgetting \(h^2\) or assuming \(h = 1\). With \(h = 1\) you would have got \(M_1 = -6\) – four times too large.
steps.insight: Do not forget the factor \(\frac{6}{h^2}\)!

steps.text: With many points the moment equations are written as a matrix. For the natural spline with \(n - 1\) interior nodes:
steps.explanation:
The matrix is tridiagonal: only the main diagonal and the two neighbouring diagonals are occupied.

And it is strictly diagonally dominant: in each row \(4 > 1 + 1\). It follows (see “Iterative Solvers for Linear Systems”): the matrix is invertible, the spline always exists and is unique.
steps.insight: The spline matrix is tridiagonal and strictly diagonally dominant ⇒ unique solution.

steps.text: Tridiagonal systems are solved with a slimmed-down Gaussian elimination, the Thomas algorithm:
steps.explanation:
1. Forward: in each row only a single entry (the one below the diagonal) has to be eliminated. The multiplier is \(\frac{1}{\text{current diagonal element}}\).
2. Backward: back substitution, where each row has only one neighbour.

Cost: about \(8n\) operations instead of \(\frac{2}{3}n^3\) for a full matrix. For \(n = 1000\) points that is \(8000\) instead of almost a billion operations.

Thanks to diagonal dominance no pivoting is needed – the method is stable anyway.

So the spline is computed in fractions of a second even for millions of points.
steps.insight: Thomas algorithm: Gauss for tridiagonal matrices in \(O(n)\) – without pivoting.

steps.text: Quick check: solve the tridiagonal system with the Thomas algorithm:
steps.insight: In tridiagonal systems every elimination and substitution row has only one neighbour.

steps.text: Why does the natural spline look so “natural”? It has a remarkable minimal property:
steps.formula: \int_{x_0}^{x_n} s''(x)^2\, dx \;\le\; \int_{x_0}^{x_n} g''(x)^2\, dx \quad \text{for every } C^2 \text{ function } g \text{ through the same points}
steps.explanation:
The integral \(\int (g'')^2\) roughly measures the total curvature of the curve – for a bent beam it is proportional to the bending energy.

So among all smooth curves through the given points, the natural spline is the “least bent”. This is exactly the shape the wooden strip takes on by itself, because it minimises its energy.

This explains why splines do not oscillate unnecessarily: every extra oscillation would cost curvature.
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Why splines are so good
steps.insight: Minimal property: among all interpolating \(C^2\) curves, the natural spline has the smallest total curvature.

steps.text: How accurate are cubic splines? For smooth functions (with suitable boundary conditions):
steps.explanation:
Order 4: halving the step size ⇒ one sixteenth of the error.

Test with \(\sin x\) on \([0, \pi]\) (here the natural spline fits perfectly, because \(\sin'' = 0\) at both ends):
\(\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{subintervals} & \text{linear spline} & \text{cubic spline} \\ \hline 4 & 7.0 \cdot 10^{-2} & 1.1 \cdot 10^{-3} \\ 8 & 1.9 \cdot 10^{-2} & 6.3 \cdot 10^{-5} \\ 16 & 4.8 \cdot 10^{-3} & 3.9 \cdot 10^{-6} \end{array}\)

Linear: factor 4 per halving. Cubic: factor 16. With only 16 pieces the cubic spline is accurate to 6 digits – the linear spline would need over 1000 pieces for that.

Caution: if the natural boundary condition does not match the function (\(f'' \neq 0\) at the ends), the error near the ends is only \(O(h^2)\). Then the clamped boundary condition is better.
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Why splines are so good
steps.insight: Cubic splines have error order 4 – very accurate with few nodes.

steps.text: A comparison of the interpolation methods at a glance:
steps.explanation:
“Local” means: if you change one data point, the curve changes only nearby. For the cubic spline the change theoretically affects everything, but it dies out very quickly (by about a factor of \(0.27\) per node).

That is why cubic splines are the standard for interpolating many data points. Computer graphics uses related constructions (B-splines, Bézier curves) where the shape is controlled via control points.
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Why splines are so good
steps.insight: Cubic splines: smooth, accurate, cheap and almost local – the standard for many data points.

steps.text: Quick check: is the following function a cubic spline for the nodes \(0, 1, 2\)?
steps.explanation:
Check at the node \(x = 1\):
• Value: left \(1^3 = 1\), right \(1 + 0 = 1\) ✓
• Slope: left \(3x^2 = 3\), right \(3 + 6(x - 1) - 3(x - 1)^2 = 3\) ✓
• Curvature: left \(6x = 6\), right \(6 - 6(x - 1) = 6\) ✓

Yes, \(s\) is a cubic spline (piecewise cubic, \(C^2\)).

Is it even natural? End curvatures: \(s''(0) = 6 \cdot 0 = 0\) ✓ and \(s''(2) = 6 - 6 \cdot 1 = 0\) ✓. Yes – it is the natural spline for the values \(0, 1, 6\) at the nodes \(0, 1, 2\).
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Why splines are so good
steps.insight: Spline check: at each interior node compare value, first and second derivative from the left and right.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Splines are piecewise polynomials. They avoid Runge's phenomenon.

2. Linear spline: polygonal line, error \(\le \frac{h^2}{8}\max|f''|\), but kinks.

3. Cubic spline: piecewise cubic, \(C^2\), \(4n\) unknowns, \(4n - 2\) conditions + 2 boundary conditions (natural, clamped, periodic, not-a-knot).

4. Moment method: \(M_i = s''(x_i)\), equations \(M_{i-1} + 4M_i + M_{i+1} = \frac{6}{h^2}(y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1})\), then the pieces with the standard formula.

5. The linear system is tridiagonal and diagonally dominant: uniquely solvable in \(O(n)\) (Thomas algorithm).

6. Minimal property: smallest total curvature \(\int (s'')^2\). Error order \(O(h^4)\).
steps.insight: Key message: connecting many data points smoothly? Cubic spline.

steps.text: What comes next? Interpolation is a tool for many other tasks. The first of them: computing integrals.
steps.explanation:
In the lesson “Numerical Integration” the function under the integral is replaced by an interpolating polynomial (or piecewise by several) and this is integrated exactly:
• linear interpolation gives the trapezoidal rule,
• quadratic interpolation gives Simpson's rule.

The error orders you met here (\(O(h^2)\), \(O(h^4)\)) show up there again.
steps.insight: Next step: integrating interpolating polynomials – numerical quadrature.
